newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac urges crackdown on racism.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac urges crackdown on racism.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac vowed on Tuesday to crack down on discrimination and punish racism in a thinly-veiled attack on the anti-immigrant far-right National Front party.
Chirac used an International Human Rights Day address to say he would not let "those who call for exclusion, hatred and violence be sheltered by freedom of expression".

He did not name the National Front of Jean-Marie Le Pen, but the threat was clearly aimed at the far-right leader who recently caused an outcry by espousing racial inequality. Le Pen wants to all immigrants sent home and advocates giving French citizens preference over foreigners for jobs.
"When discriminatory attitudes or practices, racist or xenophobic words are being expressed in our country, they must be singled out, prosecuted and punished," he said.
Chirac also took a swipe at sects, who have come under close scrutiny after the mass suicide-cum-murder of members of the Order of the Solar Temple a year ago.
"We will not let certain groups enslave souls and destroy free will by sheltering behind the freedom of creed and cult," he said.
Politicians across the spectrum pounced on Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in last year's presidential election, after he said that racial inequality was a fact.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe described him as "deeply, almost viscerally racist, antisemitic and xenophobic", but ruled against prosecuting him as current laws only punish attacks on a particular race group.
A bill to be debated in parliament early next year widens grounds for prosecution and stiffens penalties for racism.

In the Alpine city of Grenoble on Monday, eight riot police were hurt in a clash with demonstrators protesting at a visit by Le Pen to open a new National Front office. Witnesses saw at least one demonstrator injured.

Chirac urged French people not to show hostility towards the country's Moslem community after four people died in the bombing of a Paris commuter train last week. The attack bore the hallmarks of Algerian Moslem fundamentalist rebels blamed for a Paris wave of bombings which killed eight people last year.
"I know (French people) will avoid any generalisation. In no way will we fall into terrorism's trap," he said.

Chirac also called on the government to reflect on further steps to ease the social and cultural integration of legal immigrants into the country, including cutting delays in dealing with applications for French citizenship.

In his speech to the National Human Rights Commission, Chirac acknowledged that France's controversial laws to curb immigration had been criticised on human rights grounds and caused confusion, and said flaws must be corrected.
The commission has urged a wide-ranging review of the tough 1993 laws which have drawn wide criticism at home and abroad.

The government last month approved a bill to plug loopholes in the law which caused embarrassing protests by immigrants who said the 1993 crackdown deprived them of residence rights they once enjoyed and left them in a legal vacuum.
